candidates.name: dgunning/edgartools
candidates.what_it_holds: Python client (MIT, 2711 stars, active, updated 2026-09-14) that reads and structures the full SEC EDGAR archive back to 1994: 10-K/10-Q financial statements, XBRL-standardized concepts for cross-company comparison, 8-K events, 13F institutional holdings, Form 3/4/5 insider transactions, DEF 14A proxies, fund N-CSR/N-PORT reports. Not a static dataset -- a one-command pull tool for point-in-time filing data (filing timestamps are inherent to EDGAR, so this can build vintage-correct financial statement panels for ABNB/BKNG/EXPE/MAR/HLT and institutional-ownership history) without XBRL frames plumbing.
candidates.why_useful: Directly serves gap #15 (13F holdings, EDGAR XBRL tooling) and the point-in-time consensus/financials need in #4 -- gives an easy, well-maintained way to pull vintage-correct peer financials and 13F ownership snapshots at each historical filing date rather than pull-date-anchored Bloomberg exports.
candidates.size_hint: library, no bundled data (pulls live from EDGAR)

candidates.name: toddwschneider/sec-13f-filings
candidates.what_it_holds: Ruby on Rails app (MIT, 438 stars) with a schema (thirteen_fs / holdings / aggregate_holdings tables) and scripts that import and parse SEC 13F XML filings from 2014 onward for any manager CIK you specify; the live instance (13f.info) already tracks large holders such as Berkshire Hathaway quarterly. No CUSIP-ticker mapping bundled (licensing), but the parser and schema are complete.
candidates.why_useful: Turns raw 13F XML into a queryable holdings-history database -- lets us build ABNB institutional-ownership concentration/turnover history (fund entries/exits, hedge fund vs long-only mix) as a positioning read ahead of the Q4 guide, complementing the options-chain and short-interest data already held.
candidates.size_hint: app + schema, no bundled data (pulls from EDGAR)

candidates.name: martinshkreli/13F
candidates.what_it_holds: Small 13F analyzer (88 stars) that strips options-only holdings out of raw filings to isolate a fund's actual equity/stock positions, as opposed to option overlays that can distort raw 13F position counts.
candidates.why_useful: A narrower, complementary parser for cleaning 13F data before building any ABNB/peer ownership-concentration series -- useful check against sec-13f-filings output.
candidates.time_coverage: n/a (parses whatever filings are fed in)

candidates.name: CodeWritingCow/sec-web-scraper-13f
candidates.what_it_holds: Python scraper (MIT, 48 stars) for parsing 13F filings (mutual-fund holdings) directly off the SEC website.
candidates.why_useful: Alternate, simpler 13F puller if edgartools is overkill; same ownership-history use case as above.

candidates.name: OpportunityInsights/EconomicTracker
candidates.what_it_holds: Official repo (341 stars, updated 2026-09-12) backing tracktherecovery.org: anonymized aggregated data from private-sector partners (credit-card processors, payroll firms, Womply, etc.) on consumer spending, employment, and job postings, broken out by county, industry sector, and income quartile, from Jan 2020 to present, with a data dictionary and downloadable CSV/ZIP files plus the processing code.
candidates.why_useful: Exact hit on the CONTEXT.md gap #6 target (Opportunity Insights Economic Tracker card spend) -- gives a free, granular (county x income-quartile), reasonably current US consumer discretionary-spend series that can proxy travel/leisure demand strength ahead of Airbnb's US/NA nights and ADR quarters.
candidates.size_hint: multiple CSV/ZIP files, county x week granularity

candidates.name: DaWe35/Similarweb-free-API
candidates.what_it_holds: Python example (153 stars, updated 2026-08-20) hitting Similarweb's free browser-extension API endpoint (no API key required) to pull site traffic/engagement estimates for any domain.
candidates.why_useful: Directly serves gap #5 (Similarweb-like web-traffic estimates) -- a no-cost route to a time series of airbnb.com (and vrbo.com, booking.com, expedia.com) visit/engagement estimates as a demand-engagement proxy ahead of prints, without a paid Similarweb contract.
candidates.time_coverage: current snapshot only per call; would need repeated pulls to build a series

candidates.name: shihs/similarweb
candidates.what_it_holds: A Similarweb crawler (21 stars) for pulling site engagement/traffic metrics, an alternative implementation to DaWe35's.
candidates.why_useful: Backup method for the same web-traffic engagement proxy as above (gap #5) if the free-API endpoint changes.

candidates.name: DistriNet/tranco-list
candidates.what_it_holds: Source code (191 stars) generating the Tranco top-sites ranking (research-grade, manipulation-hardened, published NDSS paper); daily list generation pipeline. Actual historical daily rankings are served from tranco-list.eu (each list gets a permanent ID, so historical airbnb.com/vrbo.com/booking.com rank snapshots are retrievable), not bundled as data files in this repo.
candidates.why_useful: Named explicitly in gap #5 (Tranco / Common Crawl host-graph ranks); gives a durable, versioned, non-manipulable domain-popularity rank history for Airbnb vs. peers as an engagement-momentum proxy, and the companion tranco-python-package / tranco-list-api repos below make historical list IDs machine-pullable.
candidates.time_coverage: 2018ish-present daily lists (per tranco-list.eu; not detailed in this repo's page)
candidates.size_hint: pipeline code, not data (data hosted externally)

candidates.name: DistriNet/tranco-python-package
candidates.what_it_holds: Python package (23 stars, MIT) to fetch a Tranco list by date or permanent ID and query a domain's historical rank.
candidates.why_useful: Machine-pullable companion to the Tranco ranking generator above; lets a script reconstruct airbnb.com's rank on any specific historical date for a point-in-time engagement series.

candidates.name: openskynetwork/opensky-api
candidates.what_it_holds: Official Python/Java client (GPL-3.0, 466 stars, updated 2026-09-05) for the OpenSky Network REST API -- live and historical ADS-B flight-state vectors (position, altitude, callsign) crowd-sourced from thousands of ground receivers worldwide; OpenSky also separately publishes bulk historical Impala/Trino state-vector archives back to 2019.
candidates.why_useful: Directly serves gap #10 (airline/rail/road capacity and traffic) -- flight-count/route-frequency series into leisure-heavy airports (Cancun, Honolulu, Lisbon, Bali) can proxy inbound-travel volume and seasonality feeding Airbnb nights, independent of BTS T-100's US-only, lagged scope.
candidates.time_coverage: live + historical archive back to ~2019 (via separate Impala/Trino access, not in this repo)
candidates.size_hint: client library only; bulk historical data lives on OpenSky's own infrastructure

candidates.name: snauhaus/link_compustat_ibes
candidates.what_it_holds: Python script (18 stars, MIT) that builds a linking table between I/B/E/S (analyst estimates) and Compustat identifiers -- standard WRDS-side plumbing academics use before merging consensus-estimate history onto fundamentals.
candidates.why_useful: Relevant only if the team ever gets WRDS/I-B-E-S access (UF likely has an institutional WRDS subscription) -- would let us build a genuinely point-in-time analyst-consensus-revision history for ABNB/BKNG/EXPE (gap #4) rather than pull-date-anchored Bloomberg snapshots. No data included in the repo itself, and WRDS access is a paid/licensed academic resource, not free/open.
candidates.time_coverage: per WRDS I/B/E/S vintage (typically 1976+, monthly consensus snapshots)
candidates.license: MIT (code only; IBES/Compustat data itself is licensed via WRDS, not open)

candidates.name: cagdemir/firm-characteristics-calculation
candidates.what_it_holds: Python code (14 stars, MIT) to compute standard firm-characteristic factors by pulling from Compustat, CRSP, and IBES via WRDS.
candidates.why_useful: Same WRDS-dependent consensus-history angle as above; would only matter if WRDS access materializes before the memo deadline.

candidates.name: cutemarkets/cutemarkets-cookbook
candidates.what_it_holds: Runnable Python/TypeScript recipes (3 stars, MIT, updated 2026-08-17) for the CuteMarkets options data API: option-chain scanners, historical contract reconstruction, an explicit 'earnings implied move' recipe, and quote-quality checks.
candidates.why_useful: Gives a ready-made implied-move calculation recipe (straddle-based) that could be pointed at ABNB's own option chain around the 5 Nov print instead of hand-rolling one from the Yahoo chain already held -- but note CuteMarkets itself is a commercial data vendor, so free access may be limited (check ToS/pricing before relying on it).
candidates.time_coverage: depends on CuteMarkets API access tier
candidates.license: MIT (recipes only; underlying data is a paid vendor API)

candidates.name: unniananya/Earnings-Implied-Move-Mispricing
candidates.what_it_holds: Student research repo building a cross-sectional model of implied-vs-realized earnings-move mispricing from option straddle prices, realized post-earnings moves, volatility features, and event history; long-short backtest included.
candidates.why_useful: A worked methodology for comparing ABNB's straddle-implied 5 Nov move against realized historical post-print moves (already partly done in the reverse-DCF market-implied model per memory) -- could sanity-check or extend that sd-of-move estimate; no bundled ABNB data.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: overlaps existing options-implied-move work in docs/reverse_dcf

candidates.name: JunchiDu/pead-event-study-us-firms
candidates.what_it_holds: R event-study code testing whether post-earnings-announcement drift persists among 50 large US firms, 2000-2024, using CRSP/Compustat data (licensed, not bundled).
candidates.why_useful: A ready-made PEAD event-study framework (gap #17 methods) that could be adapted to test whether ABNB (and peers BKNG/EXPE) exhibit drift after beats/misses on nights/ADR/guide -- relevant to how the stock trades in the days after the 5 Nov print, though it requires CRSP/Compustat access we may not have.
candidates.license: unspecified (code only; CRSP/Compustat data is licensed)

candidates.name: n-white/nomadListData
candidates.what_it_holds: A 2016-vintage scrape of Nomad List city data (cost of living, internet speed, digital-nomad popularity by city) -- old and unmaintained (0 stars, last commit 2016), so treat as a single historical snapshot rather than a series.
candidates.why_useful: Weak but directly on-target for gap #16 (Nomad List / digital-nomad demand data) -- Nomad List does not otherwise expose historical downloads, so an old committed scrape is the only way to anchor a 2016 baseline for long-stay/remote-work demand by city; would need a second, more recent scrape to build any trend.

notes: Ten wildcard ideas hunted, framed as a sell-side OTA analyst's usual toolkit rather than Airbnb-specific searches: (1) IBES/analyst-consensus-history parsers -- MISS as open data (WRDS-gated; only linking-table tooling found, snauhaus/link_compustat_ibes and cagdemir/firm-characteristics-calculation -- worth revisiting only if the team secures WRDS/IBES access, otherwise dead end, same conclusion as the existing Bloomberg-workbook pull-date-anchored limitation). (2) 13F institutional-holdings parsers -- HIT: dgunning/edgartools (best-in-class, also covers XBRL/10-K/8-K/Form4, MIT, very active) plus toddwschneider/sec-13f-filings, martinshkreli/13F, CodeWritingCow/sec-web-scraper-13f as narrower alternatives; none bundle CUSIP-ticker mapping (licensing gap noted upstream). (3) Options-implied-move/straddle calculators -- weak hits (cutemarkets-cookbook depends on a paid vendor API; unniananya's mispricing repo is a methodology exercise); nothing beats what the team already has in the reverse-DCF market-implied model. (4) PEAD replication packages -- many exist (8+ found) but virtually all require licensed CRSP/Compustat/WRDS data the team may not hold; JunchiDu's 2000-2024 US event study is the cleanest framework if that access exists. (5) SEC EDGAR XBRL bulk/frames datasets -- direct-phrase search came up empty, but edgartools (found under idea #2) already covers this need with a live one-command pull back to 1994, so treat as satisfied via that repo rather than a separate bulk-file dataset. (6) Credit-card/consumer-spend panels -- HIT and notable: OpportunityInsights/EconomicTracker is an exact, currently-updated (Sep 2026) match to CONTEXT.md gap #6, with county x income-quartile US consumer spending -- flag as a priority follow-up to actually pull and test against ABNB NA nights. (7) Web-traffic/engagement estimators -- HIT: DaWe35/Similarweb-free-API (no API key, 153 stars, active) is a genuinely easy way to get Similarweb-style traffic estimates for airbnb.com and peer domains, directly serving gap #5; Tranco (DistriNet/tranco-list + tranco-python-package) gives a rank-history alternative that is more defensible (manipulation-hardened, versioned lists) if free Similarweb access proves unreliable. (8) Flight/ADS-B tracking -- HIT: openskynetwork/opensky-api, official and well-maintained, though the useful bulk historical archive lives on OpenSky's own Impala/Trino cluster rather than in this repo -- flag as a method, someone still has to build the query. (9) Cruise-line advance-booking data (NCLH as a 'book-ahead' kernel analogue, gap #18) -- clean MISS; searched 'NCLH', 'cruise line booking', 'cruise ticket sales', 'cruise industry booking data' -- nothing but unrelated repos reusing the NCLH string (North Carolina Legal Hackers, dashboards named NCLH) or empty results; likely genuinely absent from GitHub, would need SEC-filing text-mining of NCLH's own 10-Qs (their 'advance ticket sales' balance-sheet line) via a generic EDGAR tool like edgartools rather than a purpose-built repo. (10) FX-forward/European consumer card-spend panels -- MISS on GitHub via the queries tried ('FX forward historical rates dataset', 'consumer card spend index', 'card spend index'); did not retry with country-specific terms (BBVA, CaixaBank, Norway/Portugal central-bank names) that CONTEXT.md gap #6 already names as specific leads -- a follow-up scout should search those country names directly rather than generic English financial-jargon queries, which returned mostly noise or empty pages throughout this run.
